AML.T0036|inherited|1.note: adjudicated: The two verifiers substantively agree -- the row records adopt=false and both accept that no edge should be emitted -- so the only real dispute is which verdict label carries that outcome. Under the stated rule the label is kill: d3f:accesses(d3f:Resource) is not plainly supported by the technique's definition, because d3f:Resource is a near-root catch-all ('any physical or virtual component of limited availability within a computer system ... files ... network sockets ... memory areas') that discriminates nothing, and an edge from it would attach essentially every resource-oriented defense to this technique -- exactly the false-inference harm the crosswalk exists to prevent. The technique's actual named targets are already carried by more specific rows on this same technique: d3f:Database (mapping|0, 'enterprise databases such as SQL Server'), d3f:CollaborativeSoftware (mapping|1), d3f:CodeRepository (inherited|0), and d3f:WebFileResource (inherited|2, SharePoint/Confluence). The upholder is not wrong on the merits -- adopt=false is the correct call and the non-answer policy is working -- but returning 'uphold' on a row whose relation is over-generic risks a downstream consumer reading the verdict as a licence to emit the edge, and the rule directs kill for any relation the definition does not plainly support. Killing is both rule-consistent and the safe label; the outcome (no edge) is what both verifiers wanted.
